linkedin.about: Sahil Bloom is the New York Times Bestselling author of The 5 Types of Wealth: A Transformative Guide to Design Your Dream Life. Sahil is an inspirational writer and entrepreneur, captivating millions of people every week through his book, social insights, and bi-weekly newsletter, The Curiosity Chronicle. His debut non-fiction book, The 5 Types of Wealth, was an instant New York Times, USA Today, and Sunday Times Bestseller. Apple CEO Tim Cook called it "a powerful call to action to think deeply about what lights you up—and a guide for how to build a life of meaning and purpose around those things." The book is a unique blend of strategies, tactics, and actionable insights, enabling readers to make real, positive changes and lead healthier, wealthier lives. It has been translated into 39 languages and sold over 500,000+ copies worldwide. Sahil is also an entrepreneur and owner of SRB Holdings, a personal holding company, and the Managing Partner of SRB Ventures, a $10 million venture investment firm committed to investing in and accelerating the most compelling startups in the world. Prior to launching SRB Ventures in January 2022, Sahil was an early-stage investor in 40+ startups across the technology landscape, including multiple unicorns. Previously, Sahil spent seven years as a private equity investor and served on the board of several middle market companies during that period. Sahil graduated from Stanford University with an M.A. in Public Policy (2014) and a B.A. in Economics & Sociology (2013). While at Stanford, he was a four-year member on the Stanford Baseball Team (2009-2013), twice helping to guide the team to NCAA Super Regional appearances (top-16 finishes). Additionally, Sahil earned two PAC-12 All-Academic Team awards and twice received the Bruce R. Cameron Memorial Award, given annually to a student-athlete exhibiting excellence in athletics, academics, and leadership. Academically, Sahil was advised in his pursuits by former Secretary of State Dr. Condoleezza Rice.

Your energy creates your reality.

(And It becomes your destiny.)

I'm convinced of this.

Give your energy to stress, complaints, and negative people. They will grow.
Give your energy to ambitions, gratitude, and positive people. They will grow.

Whatever you feed gets bigger.

Choose wisely.

——

My entire life changed with one realization.

(The people I admired just started.)

They weren't smarter.
They weren't luckier.
They weren't specially chosen.

They simply had the courage to start.

The ones who didn't overthink it.
Who put their ego aside.
Who walked toward uncertainty.
Who kept showing up.

The answer is found in the action.

Start ugly. Go do the damn thing.

(Most people never do.)

"Stop trying to look polished. Start trying to stay in motion."

Emotional control is the ultimate power.

(Few people actually have it.)

I'm convinced of this:

The ability to remain unshaken by the minor inconveniences of life puts you ahead of 95% of people.

Traffic.
A rude email.

Not every season needs to be your best.

(Some are just for surviving.)

The older I get, the more I realize that life has seasons.

Some seasons are for building.
Some are for healing.
Some are for just surviving.

You don't have to win every single chapter for the whole story to turn out well.

Here's what I've learned:

When you demand peak performance from a healing chapter, you punish yourself for doing the work that chapter actually requires.

Honor the season you're in.

Stop forcing a highlight reel out of a rebuild.

The story can still turn out well.

Your feelings are temporary.

(Your decisions often aren't.)

We've all been there.

Messages sent you can't take back. 
Calls made you spent years undoing.

In the moment, the feelings felt like truth. They weren't.

Bad days pass. Anger fades. Fear settles.

The decision you make while they're loud stays long after they're quiet.

Here's what I've learned:

Never make a permanent decision based on a temporary feeling.

Just learn to pause. Take a walk. Sleep on it. Give it a minute.

You can always act tomorrow.
You can't always undo a rushed decision made today.

Learn to wait one more beat

Never make someone regret being honest.

(You won't like the long-term results.)

If someone has the courage to tell you the truth, don't punish them for it.

You can disagree.
You can feel defensive.
You can need a minute.

But if you train people to believe that honesty gets punished, they'll stop bringing you the real thing.

Every time you punish the truth, you teach silence.
Every time you receive it well, you invite more of it.

Comfort feels better in the moment.
Truth compounds over a lifetime.

Never make someone regret being honest with you.

——

“20 years from now, the only people who will remember that you worked late are your kids.”

I’m of two minds here:

1. Being present with your kids is the most important thing.

2. Having your kids see you work hard with a clear purpose is a principle they’ll remember forever.

It’s easy to focus on the first point and lose sight of the second.

Understanding, navigating, and balancing the tension across the two is how I believe you ultimately “win” the game.

The reality is that not everyone has the luxury of building a life where they are going to be constantly present with their kids.

Some have to work two jobs or long hours to provide for them.

Some are working long hours to build towards some ambitious future.

Focus on what you can control:

1. Include your kids in the WHY: Make sure they know why you’re working hard, why you’re away, and why it’s important.

2. When you’re around, be present: Say yes to play and give them your full energy and attention. Time and energy are not the same thing. Your energy is what counts.

What do you think?

Let me explain:

All my notes were spread across physical notebooks with no way to search across them. It delayed my launch by months.

The Kindle Scribe changed all of that for book two.

I get the same science-backed benefits of handwriting but with the power of AI. I can quickly search for specific ideas across all my notebooks. I can even have its AI synthesize ideas across everything I’ve written.

It’s the one device I never leave home without, because who knows when ideas might strike. No matter what your work looks like, I cannot recommend it highly enough.

Saturday in my life (as a 35-year-old dad):

- 4:20am wake up
- Solo sub-2:50 marathon
- Full family day
- 8:30pm bedtime

I took that marathon failure last weekend personally. So I drove back to the course and started running in the dark by myself. And I got it done. 2:48:47 (6:26 per mile). No, it doesn’t “count” but when I say I’m going to do something, I do it. Full stop.

Never bet against the person who just keeps showing up.

It was tiring going into a full family day after the run, but honestly, these are the days I dreamed of. I’ll always find energy for them.

The good old days are happening right now.
